claim: tldraw's maintainer reports a significant increase in contributions generated entirely by AI tools.
quote: Like many other open-source projects on GitHub, we've recently seen a significant increase in contributions generated entirely by AI tools.

claim: According to tldraw, most AI-generated PRs lack context and codebase understanding, and their authors rarely follow up.
quote: most suffer from incomplete or misleading context, misunderstanding of the codebase, and little to no follow-up engagement from their authors

claim: Rust maintainers describe slop contributions as a DDoS on maintenance and moderation capacity.
quote: To put it bluntly, it feels like DDoS against maintenance and moderation capacity.

claim: Astropy maintainers report that even obviously bad AI-generated PRs still cost triage time.
quote: even if these are obviously dead on arrival, they still take time to triage

claim: Some AI-generated PRs look legitimate and reveal their flaws only during in-depth review, so triage alone cannot catch them.
quote: Some of them may look legit at first glance, only revealing flaws when one dive into the code/logic during the review process.

claim: LLVM's policy states that AI tools shift effort from the implementer to the reviewer.
quote: While new tools enable more development, it shifts effort from the implementor to the reviewer

claim: Linux kernel guidelines treat tool-driven contribution volume as a pressure on scarce reviewer bandwidth.
quote: These tools can increase the volume of contributions. At the same time, reviewer and maintainer bandwidth is a scarce resource.

claim: Ghostty frames low-effort AI contributions as pushing the validation burden onto maintainers.
quote: It is rude and disrespectful to approach this boundary with low-effort, unqualified work, since it puts the burden of validation on the maintainer.

claim: scikit-learn will ban users who submit AI-generated content they don't understand, citing maintainer burden.
quote: Due to the burden put on maintainers, users submitting multiple low quality pull requests, or AI generated comments, reviews, issues, or pull requests, where the user does not show a good understanding of what they are posting, might be banned from the organisation.

claim: Zulip's AI policy is motivated by limited maintainer time.
quote: Maintainer time and attention is very limited

claim: QEMU declines contributions believed to contain AI-generated content.
quote: Current QEMU project policy is to DECLINE any contributions which are believed to include or derive from AI generated content.
context: QEMU's stated reason is legal and provenance risk, not review volume, so this is context rather than support.

claim: Godot requires autonomous AI agents to self-disclose and bans agents that don't.
quote: Agents failing to self-disclose will be banned from contributing to the project.
context: Suggests autonomous agents (not just AI-assisted humans) are submitting to large projects.

claim: tldraw closed external PRs because it considered GitHub's existing contribution-management tools inadequate.
quote: This is a temporary policy until GitHub provides better tools for managing contributions.

claim: Ghostty attributes the problem to unqualified contributors, not to AI tools themselves.
quote: It's the people, not the tools, that are the problem.
context: Contradicts framing the problem as 'AI-generated content'. The issue is unreviewed, low-understanding work.

claim: Zulip explicitly permits AI tools, so AI authorship alone isn't treated as the problem.
quote: You can use any tools that help you understand the Zulip codebase and write good code, including AI tools.

claim: curl accepts AI-assisted code, so its concern is quality and verification, not AI use.
quote: We can accept code written with the help of AI into the project

claim: curl reports that fabricated security reports stop real project work.
quote: Fake and otherwise made up security problems effectively prevent us from doing real project work and make us waste time and resources.

claim: curl's contributor guide warns that AI tools frequently produce fabricated findings.
quote: AI-based tools frequently generate inaccurate or fabricated results.

claim: curl no longer offers a bug bounty, saying bounties incentivise made-up problems that cause overload.
quote: A bug bounty gives people too strong incentives to find and make up "problems" in bad faith that cause overload and abuse.

claim: Before LLMs, simply posting a change for review signalled a potential long-term contributor.
quote: posting a change for review was a sign of interest from a potential long-term contributor

claim: The Vouch author argues that the effort of submitting a change no longer filters for trustworthy contributors.
quote: Contributors can no longer be trusted based on the minimal barrier to entry to simply submit a change.

claim: Maintainers used to review every change, a practice that AI-generated volume now strains.
quote: Prior to the advent of LLMs, open source project maintainers would often review any and all changes sent to the project

claim: Across 281 open-source AI contribution policies, 83.3% permit or encourage AI in code contributions.
quote: permission is the norm rather than the exception: 83.3% of policies permit or encourage AI in code contributions
context: Undercuts gating on AI authorship: most projects explicitly allow AI-assisted code.

claim: Most AI policies (67.3%) require a high level of human involvement, which is the property a comprehension gate tries to check.
quote: But permission comes with conditions, as 67.3% require a high level of human involvement and 43.4% assign accountability.

claim: A systematic study found ten distinct countermeasures against AI slop already in use, so the solution space is actively explored.
quote: we identify ten countermeasures against AI slop, targeting pull requests, users, and autonomous agents

claim: An empirical analysis of OSS AI policies finds that protecting scarce maintainer attention is a primary rationale.
quote: these policies seek to protect scarce maintainer attention, preserve accountability, sustain meaningful review interactions, address legal and quality concerns, and maintain pathways for newcomer learning

claim: In 11,097 repositories, AI coding-agent adoption is associated with a 3.7-point drop in newcomers' share of participation.
quote: The relative participation share of newcomers declines significantly by 3.7 percentage points (ATT = -0.037, p < 0.001)
limitations: Measures agent adoption by the repository itself, not inbound AI contributions. Supports the newcomer-pathway concern only indirectly.

claim: The same study finds no significant change in the absolute number of human contributors.
quote: AI agent adoption does not significantly change the absolute number of human contributors (ATT = 0.014, p = 0.224)
context: Tempers claims that AI drives human contributors away. The effect is on relative share.

claim: In 675 security-related agent PRs, rejections often stem from inactivity rather than code content, consistent with engagement being a useful signal.
quote: rejections often arise from social or process factors such as inactivity or missing test coverage
limitations: Different population (agent PRs, security subset). Indirect support for assumption a1.

claim: Flawed AI-generated security contributions are often merged, so review isn't catching all problems.
quote: Many flawed contributions are still merged

claim: In one dataset, reviewers expressed more neutral or positive sentiment toward AI-generated PRs than human ones.
quote: reviewers tend to express more neutral or positive emotions towards AI-generated contributions than human ones
context: Reviewer sentiment in agent-PR datasets doesn't match the frustration expressed in maintainer policies. The populations likely differ (owner-initiated agent PRs vs. unsolicited contributions).

claim: Most AI-generated PRs in the AIDev dataset receive no review at all.
quote: most AI-generated PRs receive no review and, when reviewed, are largely dominated by AI agents rather than humans
context: Suggests much agent PR volume never reaches maintainers' review queues, so the burden is concentrated in specific popular projects.

claim: Authors of PRs closed under AI or low-effort policies replied to human comments in 59.8% of cases, versus 90.2% for merged LLVM newcomer PRs. The pre-registered verdict is inconclusive.
quote: policy-closed: 52 of 87 PRs with a human comment got an author reply (reply rate 59.8%, 95% CI 49.3%–69.4%
context: Short of the pre-registered success threshold (≤ 45.1%), and the difference also exceeds the failure margin.

claim: Within LLVM, policy-closed PR authors reply nearly as often as merged newcomers (80.9% vs 90.2%), so engagement alone is a weak filter.
quote: Within LLVM only (same repository as the control): policy-closed PRs got an author reply in 38 of 47 cases (80.9%), versus 83 of 92 (90.2%) for merged LLVM newcomer PRs.

claim: Over a quarter of policy-closed PRs (33 of 120) were closed without any human comment, suggesting maintainers often close these silently.
quote: 33 of 120 policy-closed PRs received no human comment at all before closing.

claim: Astropy maintainers propose retiring 'good first issue' labels because triaging mostly unacceptable (usually AI-generated) PRs now costs more than the labels gain.
quote: the cost of triaging mostly unacceptable pull requests (nowadays usually AI slops) have outweighed any benefit
context: Triage cost is pushing projects to close newcomer on-ramps.

claim: scikit-learn proposed a label-triggered autoclose workflow, so a reviewer can dispose of a low-effort PR with one action while leaving a path to improve it.
quote: We would like to propose introducing an autoclose option for PRs that gets triggered when setting an "autoclose" label that can be removed if the PR is improved.

claim: nixpkgs maintainers noticed PRs that delete the AI-disclosure checkboxes from the PR template, and proposed closing them instantly: a cheap triage rule based on template compliance.
quote: some PRs will remove the Automation/Ai and Contribution policy checkboxes

claim: Blunt AI policies can exclude contributors with disabilities who rely on AI as assistive technology, an argument against automatic rejection based on AI use.
quote: The policies do not distinguish unaccountable delegation to AI from accountable AI-assisted or assistive use.
context: Supports keeping humans in the decision, and keying on behaviour rather than AI use.

claim: scikit-learn reports that AI tools used to create PRs ignore its automated-contributions policy, so written policies alone don't reduce inbound volume.
quote: AI tools many people use to create PRs don't care about our

claim: Authors of policy-violating PRs had opened more PRs across GitHub in the prior 30 days (median 6 vs 1), but the groups overlap heavily: the signal's AUC is only 0.64.
quote: median 6 (policy-closed) vs 1 (newcomer-merged); AUC 0.64
context: Weakens triage tools that rely on this signal, including Fossier's 'open PRs elsewhere'.

claim: Account age barely separates policy-violating authors from genuine newcomers (AUC 0.54).
quote: AUC 0.54

claim: Using the cross-repo PR signal to catch half of policy-violating PRs would also flag about 30% of genuine newcomers.
quote: 30.5% of genuine newcomer PRs would also be flagged

claim: Policy-violating PRs have much longer descriptions than genuine newcomer PRs (median 166 vs 87 words), consistent with maintainers' complaints about wordy AI output, but the separation is moderate (AUC 0.67).
quote: median 166 words (policy-closed) vs 87 words (newcomer-merged); AUC 0.67
context: Corroborates curl's 'too wordy' and Ghostty's 'overly verbose' descriptions of AI-generated submissions.

claim: Whether a PR references an issue doesn't distinguish policy-violating from genuine newcomer PRs (56% vs 58%, AUC 0.51).
quote: 55.8% of policy-closed vs 58.3% of newcomer-merged PRs; AUC (no reference → suspicious) 0.51

claim: Flagging by description length to catch half of policy-violating PRs would flag about 13% of genuine newcomers, a better trade-off than account-level signals (about 30%).
quote: 13.3% of genuine newcomer PRs would also be flagged

claim: Combining the two best cheap signals (description length and recent cross-repo PR count) without fitting reaches only AUC 0.69, below the pre-registered 0.70 threshold, and flags about 25% of genuine newcomers at half recall.
quote: refuted: combined AUC 0.69 < 0.70

claim: Two malicious axios releases were published through the maintainer's compromised npm account (March 2026).
quote: two malicious versions of axios (1.14.1 and 0.30.4) were published to the npm registry through my compromised account

claim: The malicious axios versions worked by adding a new dependency that installed a remote access trojan.
quote: Both versions injected a dependency called `plain-crypto-js@4.2.1` that installed a remote access trojan

claim: The malicious axios versions were live for about 3 hours.
quote: The malicious versions were live for about 3 hours before being removed.

claim: litellm 1.82.8 on PyPI shipped a credential-stealing .pth file (reported March 2026, 1,118 reactions).
quote: This is a supply chain compromise.

claim: The litellm attack added a file type (.pth) that executes on interpreter start, a change visible in package contents.
quote: contains a malicious `.pth` file

claim: asyncapi's malicious releases came from a compromised branch write token, not from a maintainer acting in bad faith.
quote: this is a branch write token compromise, not an insider issue

claim: TanStack reported that several of its npm latest releases were compromised (May 2026).
quote: We are actively investigating this security incident
limitations: The issue body only links to a vendor write-up; details are not in the captured text.

claim: Bun users request a minimum-release-age setting because popular packages were compromised right after release.
quote: Recently, the npm ecosystem has suffered several supply chain attacks where popular packages were compromised right after release.

claim: pnpm already ships a configuration option that delays installing new releases.
quote: Other package managers, such as [pnpm](https://github.com/pnpm/pnpm/pull/9921), have already introduced a configuration option to mitigate these risks.

claim: npm CLI users request the same release-age delay (241 reactions), citing a wave of high-profile attacks on popular npm packages.
quote: Following a wave of high-profile supply chain attacks targeting popular npm packages
limitations: The quoted sentence comes from a Socket.dev article reproduced in the issue.

claim: GitHub's Dependabot has offered a cooldown (update delay) against supply-chain attacks since July 2025.
quote: In July 2025, GitHub made Dependabot cooldown generally available as a defense against software supply chain attacks.

claim: Security concerns motivated 83 of 92 Dependabot cooldown adoptions with known motivation.
quote: We find that security concerns motivated 83 of 92 adoption events with known motivations.

claim: Adopters of cooldowns prefer simple default delays; fine-grained controls are rarely used (<10%).
quote: Early adopters therefore favor simple default delays over fine-grained controls.

claim: npm trusted publishing (OIDC) can't be used for a package's first version, so maintainers still need a token or a manual publish.
quote: it's not possible to publish the initial version of a package using OIDC, it needs to be published manually or using a token

claim: PyPI lets trusted publishing be configured before a package exists, so the gap is specific to npm.
quote: PyPI solved this by allowing a package to be configured with OIDC publishing before it exists.

claim: In the newest 60 hijacked npm packages in the OpenSSF dataset, 58 of 58 classifiable incidents carried a new install-hook signal, and only 1.3% of legitimate releases did.
quote: Incidents with a new-dependency or install-hook signal: 58 of 58 classifiable (100.0%).

claim: 56 of the 60 incidents come from one Shai-Hulud campaign wave, so the sample holds only about 5 independent attacks.
quote: Counted by campaign instead of by package, the sample contains about 5 independent attacks, far below the 15 the design intended.
context: Limits how far the supportive result generalises: it mainly shows that one worm campaign was detectable.

claim: A known hijack outside the sample (asyncapi) only modified an existing file, so it would not have triggered either signal.
quote: The asyncapi compromise (2026-07-14, outside the newest-60 sample) modified an existing file and would not have triggered either signal.

claim: Across independent hijack campaigns (2024–2026), 12 of 15 classifiable campaigns (80%) added an install-time hook, versus 1.7% of legitimate releases.
quote: Campaigns with a new-dependency or install-hook signal: 12 of 15 classifiable (80.0%, 95% CI 54.8%–93.0%).

claim: 3 of 15 classifiable campaigns only modified existing files and would evade a new-dependency or install-hook alarm.
quote: The 3 file-modification campaigns (asyncapi, node-ipc, netspeedutil) injected code into existing files and would not trigger a new-dependency or install-hook alarm.

claim: The result is sensitive to the 7 campaigns of unknown mechanism: the share could be anywhere from 55% to 86%.
quote: If all 7 unknown campaigns were non-signal cases, the share would be 12 of 22 (55%), below the 60% success threshold. If all were signal cases, it would be 19 of 22 (86%).

claim: Since May 2026, npm lets maintainers stage releases so that a human must approve each one with 2FA before it goes live.
quote: Staged publishing adds an approval step before packages go live on the npm registry.
context: Prevention instead of detection: an attacker holding only a token can stage a release but not make it live.

claim: Maintainers can require human proof-of-presence (2FA) for every publish.
quote: Staged publishing allows package maintainers to require proof-of-presence for all publishes.

claim: A package setting can forbid publishing with access tokens altogether, closing the stolen-token route that hit axios.
quote: Granular access tokens cannot be used to publish packages, regardless of their bypass 2FA setting.

claim: CI pipelines can be restricted to staging only, so even a compromised CI job can't publish without human approval.
quote: `npm stage publish` is always allowed. Choose whether this trusted publisher can also publish directly with `npm publish`

claim: Since 2024, PyPI emails maintainers when a long-lived API token uploads to a project that uses trusted publishing: a partial, platform-provided version of the alarm.
quote: even though the project has a Trusted Publisher configured.

claim: Socket's public tooling is consumer-side (scanning and gating installs). Whether it offers maintainer-side release alerts couldn't be verified.
quote: letting you scan dependencies, audit packages, and gate installs from your terminal or CI.

claim: Half of 400 popular npm packages (50.2%, CI 45–55%) published their latest release with neither trusted publishing nor staged approval, a route a stolen token could reproduce.
context: An upper bound: some of these are interactive publishes protected by 2FA.

claim: Only 31 of 400 popular packages (7.8%) use npm's staged publishing with human approval, six months after it launched.
quote: Staged with human approval: 31

claim: Even among 22 packages that were actually hijacked, 13 (59%) still publish their latest release with neither protection.
quote: Previously hijacked packages (latest release): 22 packages read. Staged with human approval: 2; trusted publishing (OIDC) only: 7; neither: 13

claim: Semantic Versioning promises that patch (and minor) releases don't break users. Package managers install such updates automatically.
quote: Patch version Z (x.y.Z | x > 0) MUST be incremented if only backward compatible bug fixes are introduced.

claim: React 16.4, a minor release, broke a user's whole codebase through a behaviour change.
quote: Our entire codebase, running perfectly on 16.3.2 is a dumpster fire as soon as we raise that dependency to 16.4.

claim: A breaking minor release of node-abort-controller forced Apollo Server's maintainer to pin versions, and affected Apollo's own users downstream.
quote: If not, I'll be pinning to `3.0.x` until we drop node v14, but this will continue to effect users of existing apollo server versions if their lockfiles are updated.

claim: A breaking minor release of floating-ui broke a user's release pipeline and cost them a weekend of debugging.
quote: Your change completely broke our release pipelines while we tracked down what changed over the weekend

claim: polished 4.3.0, a minor release, raised its required Node version to ≥ 20, breaking installs on Node 18. That's a metadata change, not a type change.
quote: Expected version ">=20". Got "18.19.0"

claim: Microsoft built API Extractor partly because users kept reporting compile breaks after 'minor' updates.
quote: People keep reporting that their code won't compile after a supposedly "minor" update.

claim: Rust has an established tool that checks each release for semver violations before publishing (about 1,700 stars), so the tool model is proven in another ecosystem.
quote: Lint your crate API changes for semver violations.

claim: Even the mature Rust tool documents classes of breaking change it can't detect. API-surface checking is inherently partial.
quote: Here are some example areas where `cargo-semver-checks` currently will not catch semver violations:

quote: Catch breaking TypeScript API changes before they ship.
context: The TypeScript type-surface niche is already being filled.

claim: ts-semver-checks explicitly aims to be 'cargo-semver-checks for TypeScript'.
